profile.summary: Judas is a very brief but incisive letter written to alert the church against false teachers who threatened to confuse the Christian faith. The author is not as interested in discussing in detail each teaching of them as in exposing their character: arrogant, immoral, greedy and resistant to authority, whose practice contradicted Christian confession. The letter insists that following this path leads to the judgment of God. At the same time, Judas calls believers to preserve the faith received, to discern the doctrinal danger and to help others not to be dragged away by this error. The authorship is traditionally attributed to Judas, brother of James and probably brother of Jesus, but the exact date and recipient remain uncertain; it was probably written after 45 AD and before 90 AD, possibly in temporal proximity to 2 Peter.
profile.setting: The letter is born in the context of the early church, when false teachers were already disturbing the people of God. Judas writes to react to a concrete crisis: people who claimed to follow Christ, but lived as libertines, treating grace as a license to sin and show contempt for authority. The letter reflects an environment in which the community needed to be remembered both the essential content of faith and the real danger of moral and doctrinal deviations. Literally, Judas is a short, direct and highly argumentative epistle, which uses examples of the Old Testament and Jewish traditions to reinforce his warning.

structure.label: Whole Letter
structure.description: The opening, the denunciation of the false teachers, the appeals to persevere in faith and final doxology form a single rhetorical movement within the single chapter.

themes: Danger of false doctrine within the church
Called to the defense of apostolic faith
readingKeys: Notice how Judas values the discourse of the false teachers less and more his moral conduct and attitude before authority.
Note the biblical and traditional examples used to show that rebellion against God always ends in judgment.
Read the letter as a pastoral call: it not only denounces the error, but also guides the church to stand firm and help the vacillating.
profile.cautions: The letter is very short and therefore focuses on a single purpose: to warn against false masters. It is not prudent to force in it secondary debates or detailed historical reconstructions that the introduction itself does not support. Since the authorship and the exact date cannot be fixed with absolute certainty, it is appropriate to talk cautiously about these points.

dossier.narratedEra: Judas' letter is addressed to the environment of the early Christian church, already with false teachers acting among believers. The notes describe an "lately converted to the faith of Christ" community, composed of Christians from both Judaism and paganism, and situated at a time when the apostles could still warn against doctrinal deviations (1:17-19). The narrated scenario, therefore, is that of the first Christian generation dealing with internal threat to faith and community life.
dossier.compositionEra: The letter was probably written after about A.D. 45, to allow the type of false teaching described to mature, and before about A.D. 90, when even a younger brother of Jesus would already be old. The tradition presented identifies the author as Judas, "Orhand of James" (1:1), and, consequently, brother of Jesus; the notes also observe that the resemblance to 2 Peter suggests composition approximately in the same period. Matthew Henry treats the epistle as "general" or "catholic," destined to the church in general, without precise individual recipient.

politics.title: Apostolic Authority as Central Dispute
politics.detail: The letter was written to meet teachers who had no respect for authority and who, according to the exposition, despised the authority of the Lord and even the apostolic warning. The conflict is more ecclesial and doctrinal than state: the dispute is over who has the authority to define faith and Christian behavior.
politics.readingImpact: Reading Judas as a defense of the authority received helps to realize that the problem is not only intellectual error, but rebellion against the order recognized by the nascent church.

politics.title: Aniality and foundational memory
politics.detail: The letter itself invokes that the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ foretold (1:17), suggesting a community that measures the truth by the apostolic tradition already transmitted. This implies a structure of leadership and normative remembrance in early Christianity.
politics.readingImpact: The reader is led to understand that Judas calls for fidelity to a previous apostolic deposit, not religious innovation.

politics.title: Improper extrapolate imperial powers
politics.detail: The sources do not describe emperors, civil governments, or state persecution in Judas. The political emphasis is internal, linked to the spiritual authority and discipline of the community.
politics.readingImpact: It avoids turning the letter into a direct commentary on imperial politics; the focus remains on the crisis of leadership and doctrine in the church.

customs.title: Mixed community of recent converts
customs.detail: Matthew Henry describes the recipients as newly converted Christians, coming from both Judaism and paganism. This suggests an environment of doctrinal formation still sensitive and vulnerable to seductive.
customs.readingImpact: The warning against false teachers gains pastoral weight: the community was still consolidating its Christian identity.

customs.title: Community life and shared meals
customs.detail: In 1:12, the notes claim that the early Christians celebrated the Lord's Supper as part of shared community meals. The image of the false teachers "participating" these meals shows the risk of corruption in the daily conviviality of the church.
customs.readingImpact: The text is not just about abstract doctrine; it touches the common table of the community and the integrity of shared worship.

customs.title: Hospitality and care for people in spiritual danger
customs.detail: Judas directs the "showing mercy" and "rescue" people in danger of deflection. The notes interpret this as a pastoral practice of cautious rapprochement with those who are vacillating or already committed to error.
customs.readingImpact: Pastoral reading becomes concrete: it is not enough to condemn error; the community must act with discernment and mercy.

customs.title: Conviviality with patronage and status without explicit prominence
customs.detail: The sources do not detail economics, social classes, work or family structure of the recipients. What appears is the devotional and ethical life of the church, especially the need for perseverance and solidarity among brothers.
customs.readingImpact: The interpreter should avoid sociological reconstructions beyond what the notes support; the available portrait is ecclesial and moral.

language.title: "Fé" as content and as an act of believing
language.detail: The notes distinguish that, in 1:3 and 1:20, "faith" is not only subjective trust, but the content of Christian belief, the doctrinal and ethical nucleus that must be kept.
language.readingImpact: This prevents a reduced reading of inner religiosity; Judas is defending the deposit of Christian truth.

language.title: A three-line list of examples and rhetorical cadence
language.detail: The exhibition highlights a sequence in three blocks in 1:5-16: biblical examples of condemnation, new denunciations of ungodly behavior and, finally, the quotation of Jewish tradition. This structure reinforces the accusatory and memorable tone of the letter.
language.readingImpact: The reader realizes that Judas uses repetition and parallelism to hammer the gravity of the case, not to narrate in a neutral way.

language.title: Images of deviation, impurity and errance
language.detail: The notes observe strong images: "Warning stars" in 1:13, reference to shackles, judgment and paths diverted. The language depicts the masters as unstable and condemned.
language.readingImpact: The metaphor reinforces moral reading: doctrinal error and disorderly life walk together.

language.title: Use of Jewish and Old Testament traditions
language.detail: Judas turns to Israel in the wilderness, to the rebellious angels, to Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam, Korah, and Enancing. The notes underline that the letter dynamically uses the Old Testament and Jewish traditions to qualify the false masters.
language.readingImpact: The context extends the letter: the author reads the church crisis in the light of ancient standards of rebellion and judgment.

language.title: Doxology as a liturgical language
language.detail: The conclusion in 1:24-25 is described as one of the most moving doxoologies of Scripture and often used in liturgical contexts. The language exalts God's power to keep believers from stumbling.
language.readingImpact: The letter ends not only in warning, but in worship, which shapes the reader's response: vigilance sustained by trust in God.

timeline.title: Apostolic generation still alive
timeline.detail: The notes indicate that the apostolic warnings about false teachers were already circulating when Judas writes, which suggests a moment still close to the activity of the apostles.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader understands 1:17-19 as a living testimony, not distant remembrance; the letter is anchored in a period when apostolic memory was still accessible.

timeline.title: Initial development of false education
timeline.detail: Matthew Henry notes that dangerous airs arose early in the church and that weeds appeared while some apostles still lived. This puts the composition in the early period of Christian expansion.
timeline.readingImpact: The letter gains historical urgency: Judas does not react to a late problem, but to a threat already visible in the formation phase of the church.

timeline.title: Probable Date Range: After AD 45 and Before AD 90
timeline.detail: The introduction of Tyndale proposes an approximate interval for the essay, without fixing the exact date. The reason is both the time needed for the problem to mature and the likely aging of Judas.
timeline.readingImpact: It avoids chronological dogmatism; the letter should be read as a document of the early church, but not with absolute datable precision.

timeline.title: Possible simultaneity with 2 Peter
timeline.detail: Notes suggest that the close relationship between 2 Peter and Judas may indicate written at a similar time. This is not affirmed as a proven fact, but as a literary and historical possibility.
timeline.readingImpact: The parallel helps to perceive a common environment of controversy, without forcing the reader to harmonize speculative chronologies.

timeline.title: Enoch and the intertestamentary tradition
timeline.detail: The quotation of 1 Enoch in 1:14-15 shows that Judas dialogues with preserved Jewish traditions between the Old and New Testaments. The notes mention that there are apocalyptic books attributed to Enoch in this period.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader sees that Judas operates in a wider Jewish world than only the Hebrew canon, which clarifies the texture of the argument.

investigation: The sources do not offer concrete data on empire, rulers, civil conflicts, or political geography specific to the recipient.
There is no detailed description of profession, domestic economy, family structures or social classes of readers; social reconstruction must remain modest.
The traditional authorship is attributed to Judas, brother of Jesus and James, but the note presents this as a traditional identification, not as an independent external proof.
The relationship with 2 Peter is mentioned as suggestive and therefore remains in the field of literary debate.
The Jewish traditions used by Judas are pointed out by the notes, but their exact use and reception in the community remain partially inferential.

The coverage of the notes is selective and focuses on the purpose of the letter, the characterization of the false teachers and in biblical and Jewish parallels; this limits broader reconstructions of everyday life.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends only on the notes provided and therefore does not attempt to complete gaps with external knowledge. The sources are strongly focused on theology, pastoral warning and biblical parallels; therefore, there is little direct information about political scenario, economic life, family organization or non-litigeral customs. Where there are inferences, they were marked as interpretation; where the relationship is only suggested, as the proximity to 2 Peter, was marked as debated. It is also appropriate to distinguish the narrated time from the letter to the early church under threat of false masters - from the likely time of composition, situated approximately between the middle of the 1st century and before AD 90. Finally, the historical reading presented here is conscious of the confessional use of the notes, but seeks to keep the focus on what they effectively affirm.
